extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated general readers and students/practitioners of comparative anatomy and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: An 1880 lecture/article surveying cultural practices of voluntary bodily alteration (deformity) across many peoples, classifying them, discussing motives, methods, materials, social meaning, and effects. Intended as an ethnographic/anthropological popular-science essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Deformity is spoken of "in the sense of alteration of the natural form of any part of the body."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition to delimit the subject: includes any voluntary alteration of natural form (superficial or structural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by part affected
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most convenient classification of these customs will be one which is based upon the part of the body affected by them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize descriptions/evaluations by anatomical region (hair/skin appendages; nose, lips, ears; teeth; skull and bony framework). The article follows this structure and gives detailed examples under each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence versus transience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Alterations once made in the form of the body can not be discarded or modified in the lifetime of the individual... such alterations have the strongest possible tendency to be reproduced generation after generation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between fashions that are changeable (dress, temporary hair styles) and bodily alterations that are essentially permanent and therefore have stronger cultural persistence and long-term consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/psychological motive: conformity and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing motive leading to continuation of such fashions is "the desire to conform to common usage, and not to appear singular."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing why a custom persists, prioritize social imitation and conformity as primary drivers; many practices spread because people imitate peers rather than for practical reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other motives (religious, hygienic, aesthetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fashions "have become associated with religious or superstitious observances," some have been thought to be "hygienic in motive," and "most have some relation to conventional standards of improved personal appearance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple, sometimes overlapping motives for body modification: ritual/religion, purported health/hygiene, and culturally specific aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of malleability by tissue type
rubrics_metrics.description: Some parts (hair, nails, skin appendages) are treated as comparatively superficial and flexible; others (skull, bony framework, internal organs) when altered produce permanent structural changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate customs according to whether they involve flexible/external tissues (more reversible/minor) versus hard/bony structures (permanent, with physiological consequences). The essay explicitly contrasts these classes and treats the latter as more significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of manipulation: hair and appendages as primary domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Hair "lends itself to various methods of treatment" and has been a temptation in all conditions of civilization for change in length, arrangement, and even color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect high diversity of fashions applied to hair and easily-manipulated appendages; hair practices are frequent indicators of fashion and change more readily than bony alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical inconvenience constrains custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical inconveniences (e.g., inordinate nail length, bone through nostrils forcing open the mouth) can restrict the geographical or social extent of a custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging sustainability or diffusion of a practice, consider its practical costs (hygiene, breathing, eating, manual tasks) as limiting factors; customs that impose major inconveniences tend to be localized or ritualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials & techniques shape form
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications often require "flint knives, pieces of splintered bone or shell," wires, wooden blocks, copper, brass plugs, etc.; the chosen materials and tools determine visible form and magnitude of deformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and evaluate the instruments and materials used (bone, wood, copper, lime, dyes, drilling) since they directly affect the attainable shapes, durability, and health consequences. The article provides many material-specific examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body sites as ornament foundations (nose, lips, ears, teeth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nose, the lips, and the ears "have, in almost all races, offered great temptations to be used as foundations for the display of ornament," often needing boring, cutting, or alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these body parts as frequent loci of ornamental deformation; evaluate customs by how they alter function and appearance (e.g., nostril-stopping bone affecting speech/breathing; lip blocks elongating lip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social meaning: status and exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The size/possession of certain ornaments is linked to social status (e.g., "larger lip-blocks... each enlargement adds to the lady's social status; the privilege... is not extended to female slaves").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess modifications not just for form but for their role in hierarchy, status display, and social differentiation (including restrictions by class or servitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gendered distribution of practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many customs show sex-specific patterns (e.g., among some tribes women are shaved while men cultivate elaborate hair; Thlinkeet women wear large lip-blocks; some labrets are practised only by men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and analyze differences in practices between men and women: who performs, who is expected to bear certain modifications, and how this maps to social roles and meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and rite-of-passage timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain operations are performed at particular ages or associated with initiation: e.g., Esquimaux lip piercing "performed on approaching manhood," or lip-plugs inserted in children and enlarged with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a custom, note the typical age(s) at which modifications occur and their relation to rites of passage or maturity; timing affects permanence and cultural significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional variation & convergent development
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar customs occur in distant races (e.g., bone-nose ornaments in Australia and in Prince William's Sound) — either from common origin or independent development: "a strange phenomenon" requiring explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming common origin from superficial similarity; consider independent cultural convergence and local meanings. Comparative claims should be made cautiously and supported by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dental modification practices and aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Front teeth may be chipped, filed, stained black, drilled and inlaid, or extracted according to local fashion (examples from Africa, Malay region, Java, Borneo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dental practices as a distinct category with particular techniques (chipping, filing, staining, drilling/inlays) and cultural aesthetics; note functional ramifications and diversity of decorative patterns.
